title: The Lighthouse · 2
paragraphs: She seemed to have shriveled a little, Mr. Ramsay thought. She looked rather thin and wispy, but not unattractive. He liked her. There had been some talk once of her marrying William Bankes, but nothing had come of it. His wife had been fond of her. He had been a little bad-tempered at breakfast, too. And then, and then—this was one of those moments when an enormous need drove him, without his knowing what it was, to go up to any woman and force her, he did not care how, so great was his need, to give him what he wanted: sympathy.
Was anyone looking after her? he asked. Did she have everything she wanted?

“Oh, I have everything, thanks,” Lily Briscoe said nervously. No; she could not do it. She should have floated away at once on some wave of warm, expansive sympathy: the pressure on her was tremendous. Yet she stayed stuck. An awful pause followed. They both looked at the sea. Why, Mr. Ramsay thought, should she look at the sea when I am standing here? She said she hoped it would be calm enough for them to land at the Lighthouse. The Lighthouse! The Lighthouse! What has that got to do with anything? he thought impatiently. And instantly, with the force of some primeval gust (for really he could not hold it in any longer), a groan broke from him—such a groan that any other woman in the whole world would have done something, said something. Any woman except me, Lily thought, lashing out at herself bitterly: I am not a woman at all, presumably, but a peevish, bad-tempered, dried-up old maid.

Mr. Ramsay let out the fullest of sighs. He waited. Wasn’t she going to say anything? Couldn’t she see what he wanted from her? Then he told her he had a particular reason for wanting to go to the Lighthouse. His wife used to send things to the men there. The lighthouse keeper had a son, a poor boy with a tubercular hip. He gave a deep sigh. He gave a meaningful sigh. What Lily wished, and all she wished, was that this enormous flood of grief, this hunger for sympathy that could never be satisfied, this demand that she hand herself over to him completely—and even then he would have sorrows enough to keep her supplied forever—would leave her alone, would be turned aside (she kept looking at the house, hoping someone would interrupt) before its current swept her away.

“Trips like this,” said Mr. Ramsay, scraping the ground with the toe of his boot, “are very painful.” Still Lily said nothing. (She is a block of wood, she is a stone, he said to himself.) “They are very exhausting,” he said, looking at his beautiful hands with a sickly look that turned her stomach (he was acting, she felt; this great man was making a drama of himself). It was horrible, it was indecent. Would they never come? she asked herself, for she could not bear this enormous weight of sorrow, could not hold up these heavy drapes of grief (he had taken on a pose of extreme frailty; he even tottered a little as he stood there) a moment longer.

Still she could say nothing. The whole horizon seemed swept clean of things to talk about. She could only feel, in amazement, as Mr. Ramsay stood there, how his gaze seemed to fall mournfully over the sunny grass and stain it, and how it cast a veil of black mourning crape over the ruddy, drowsy, entirely contented figure of Mr. Carmichael, reading a French novel in a deck chair—as if such a life, flaunting its well-being in a world of sorrow, were enough to stir up the gloomiest thoughts of all. Look at him, he seemed to be saying, look at me; and in fact, all the time, what he was feeling was, Think of me, think of me. Oh, if only that bulk could be floated over beside them, Lily wished; if only she had set up her easel a yard or two closer to him! A man, any man, would stop this outpouring, would put an end to these laments. She was a woman, and she had provoked this horror; as a woman, she should have known how to deal with it. It counted immensely against her, as a woman, to stand there dumb. One said—what did one say?—Oh, Mr. Ramsay! Dear Mr. Ramsay! That was what that kind old lady who sketched, Mrs. Beckwith, would have said at once, and rightly. But no. They stood there, cut off from the rest of the world. His immense self-pity, his demand for sympathy, poured out and spread in pools at her feet, and all she did, miserable sinner that she was, was to draw her skirts a little closer around her ankles, so as not to get wet. She stood there in complete silence, gripping her paintbrush.

Heaven be praised, over and over! She heard sounds in the house. James and Cam must be coming. But Mr. Ramsay, as if he knew his time was running short, bore down on her lonely figure with the immense pressure of all his concentrated sorrow—his age, his frailty, his desolation—when suddenly, tossing his head impatiently, in his annoyance (for, after all, what woman could resist him?), he noticed that his bootlaces were untied. And remarkable boots they were, too, Lily thought, looking down at them: sculpted; colossal; like everything Mr. Ramsay wore, from his frayed tie to his half-buttoned vest, unmistakably his own. She could picture them walking to his room by themselves, expressing, even in his absence, his pathos, his surliness, his bad temper, his charm.

“What beautiful boots!” she exclaimed. She was ashamed of herself. To praise his boots when he had asked her to comfort his soul; when he had shown her his bleeding hands, his torn heart, and asked her to pity them—and then to say, cheerfully, “Ah, but what beautiful boots you wear!”—deserved, she knew, total annihilation in one of his sudden roars of temper. She looked up, expecting to get it.

Mr. Ramsay smiled instead. The pall, the drapes, the infirmities all dropped off him. Ah yes, he said, raising his foot so she could look, these were first-rate boots. Only one man in England could make boots like that. Boots, he said, were among the chief curses of the human race. “Bootmakers,” he exclaimed, “make it their business to cripple and torture the human foot.” No people on earth were more stubborn and contrary. He had spent the better part of his youth getting boots made as boots ought to be made. She would please notice (up went his right foot, then his left) that she had never before seen boots of quite that shape. And the leather was the finest in the world. Most leather was mere brown paper and cardboard. Pleased with himself, he gazed at his foot, which was still in the air. They had arrived, she felt, at a sunny island where peace made its home, where sanity was in charge and the sun never stopped shining: the blessed island of good boots. She felt a warmth toward him. “Now let’s see whether you can tie a knot,” he said. He brushed aside her feeble method with scorn and demonstrated his own invention. Tie it once and it would never come undone. Three times he knotted her shoe; three times he unknotted it.

Why, at this completely inappropriate moment, when he was bending over her shoe, should she be so tormented by sympathy for him? As she bent down too, the blood rushed to her face, and, thinking of how hard she had been (she had called him a playactor), she felt her eyes swell and sting with tears. Busy like this, he seemed to her a figure of infinite pathos. He tied knots. He bought boots. There was no helping Mr. Ramsay on the journey he was making. But now, just as she wanted to say something, could perhaps have said something, here they were—Cam and James. They appeared on the terrace. They came slowly, trailing side by side, a serious, melancholy pair.

But why did they have to come like _that_? She could not help feeling annoyed with them. They might have come more cheerfully; they might have given him what she, now that they were leaving, would have no chance to give him. For she felt a sudden emptiness, a frustration. Her feeling had come too late. There it was, ready, but he no longer needed it. He had turned into a very distinguished elderly man who had no need of her whatsoever. She felt snubbed. He slung a knapsack over his shoulders. He handed out the parcels—there were a number of them, badly tied, in brown paper. He sent Cam for a cloak. He looked every inch a leader getting ready for an expedition. Then, wheeling around, he led the way down the path with his firm military step, in those wonderful boots, carrying brown paper parcels, his children following him. They looked, she thought, as if fate had given them over to some stern undertaking, and they went to meet it, still young enough to be drawn along obediently in their father’s wake, but with a paleness in their eyes that made her feel they were silently suffering something beyond their years. So they passed the edge of the lawn, and it seemed to Lily that she was watching a procession go by, drawn on by some pressure of shared feeling which made it—faltering and flagging as it was—a little company bound together, and strangely impressive to her. Politely, but very distantly, Mr. Ramsay raised his hand and saluted her as they passed.

But what a face, she thought, and at once the sympathy she had not been asked to give began troubling her, looking for a way out. What had made it like that? Thinking, night after night, she supposed—about the reality of kitchen tables, she added, remembering the symbol Andrew had given her when she was vague about what Mr. Ramsay actually thought about. (He had been killed instantly by a splinter of shell, she reminded herself.) The kitchen table was something visionary and austere; something bare, hard, not decorative. There was no color to it; it was all edges and angles; it was uncompromisingly plain. But Mr. Ramsay always kept his eyes fixed on it, never let himself be distracted or fooled, until his face too became worn and ascetic and shared in this unadorned beauty which impressed her so deeply. Then, she recalled (standing where he had left her, holding her brush), worries had worn at it—less nobly. He must have had his doubts about that table, she supposed: whether the table was a real table; whether it was worth the time he gave it; whether he was able, after all, to find it. He had had doubts, she felt, or he would have asked less of people. That was what they talked about late at night sometimes, she suspected; and then the next day Mrs. Ramsay looked tired, and Lily flew into a rage with him over some absurd little thing. But now he had nobody to talk to about that table, or his boots, or his knots; and he was like a lion seeking whom he might devour, and his face had that touch of desperation, of exaggeration, which alarmed her and made her pull her skirts around her. And then, she recalled, there was that sudden revival, that sudden flare (when she praised his boots), that sudden return of energy and interest in ordinary human things. That too passed and changed (for he was always changing, and hid nothing) into that other, final phase which was new to her, and which had, she admitted, made her ashamed of her own irritability. It seemed then as if he had shed his worries and ambitions, and the hope of sympathy and the desire for praise; as if he had entered some other region and was being drawn on, as if by curiosity, in silent conversation, whether with himself or with someone else, at the head of that little procession, out of one’s reach. An extraordinary face! The gate banged.
